concepts.definition: A list that splits a project into small jobs you can test one at a time.
concepts.example: The wandering cat project splits into seven goals: floor, walking, staying on the screen, star, talking, sound and explosion.
concepts.pitfall: Building all the blocks in one go and only trying at the end; when something breaks, you cannot find which block is the culprit.

concepts.definition: The habit of running the game again from the beginning after every small change and checking the result.
concepts.example: Straight after adding the explosion block, you press B and see the explosion.
concepts.pitfall: Not restarting the game after changing the blocks; the stage runs the old version.

concepts.definition: The response the game shows when the player does something: an explosion, a sound, a shake or a message.
concepts.example: When you press B, an explosion plus a short beep show the player that the key worked.
concepts.pitfall: Choosing an explosion position outside the stage; if it is outside x 0-160, y 0-120, you cannot see the explosion.

concepts.definition: There are three kinds of sound block: beep (Hz and ms), note (for example A4) and a ready-made melody.
concepts.example: A 300 Hz beep for 120 ms gives a short click; the start melody plays a three-note intro.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking note blocks lined up one after another will play in order; each sound block starts at once, so the three notes are heard at the same time.

concepts.definition: You can put as many blocks as you like in the event under a button; separate events for the same button also run.
concepts.example: The talking and melody blocks can go together inside the A event.
concepts.pitfall: Writing two separate events for the same button; both run and it gets confusing what causes what.

quiz.prompt:
What do you hear when the A button is pressed?

```
when A button is pressed
  play note C4 for 250 ms
  play note E4 for 250 ms
  play note G4 for 250 ms
```
options: The three notes play one after another, 750 ms in total
The three notes play at the same time, for about 250 ms
No sound comes out; you need a melody block for sound
quiz.explanation: Sound blocks start their sound the moment they run and do not wait for each other to finish. The three blocks run in the same frame, so the three notes are heard at the same time. Note blocks make a sound on their own too; a melody block is not needed.

quiz.prompt:
The explosion should happen when the B button is pressed, but it happens when A is pressed. Which is the bug?

```
1  when A button is pressed
2    kedi says "Hello!" for 2 seconds
3    yellow explosion at x 80 y 60
4  when B button is pressed
5    shake screen for 300 ms
```
options: Line 2: the talking block should be deleted
Line 3: it should be a red explosion instead of yellow
Line 3: the explosion block is inside the A event; it should be moved into the B event
Line 5: the shake block should come before the explosion
quiz.explanation: The blocks under an event only run in that event. The explosion block is connected to the A event, so it explodes when A is pressed. Once it is moved, it runs with B. There is nothing wrong with the talking, colour or shake blocks.

quiz.prompt: When the B button is pressed, the shake screen for 300 ms block runs. The game draws 60 frames a second, so about how many frames does the shake last?
quiz.explanation: 300 ms = 0.3 seconds. Time x frames per second = 0.3 x 60 = 18 frames. To turn milliseconds into seconds, you divide by 1000.

quiz.prompt: What happens if you write two separate event blocks for the same button (for example B)?
options: Only the one you wrote first runs
Only the one you wrote last runs
quiz.explanation: Each event block waits on its own; when you press B, both are triggered. So that things do not get mixed up, it is tidier to write a single event for each button and put the jobs in order inside it.

quiz.prompt: What is the safest way to develop a project with seven goals?
options: Build all the blocks and run it once at the end
Do the sounds and effects first and leave the movement until last
When there is a bug, delete all the blocks and start again
Finish one goal, run it to try it, then move on to the next goal
quiz.explanation: Trying after every step shows you that, when something breaks, the culprit is the block you added last. Building everything at once makes the bug hard to find; deleting and starting again wastes the parts that work.
